findings.text: The NUMA worker only considers migratable ranges with suitable policy, excluding huge-table and mixed-map ranges, read-only file-backed ranges, ranges without an owning address space, and ranges reported as inaccessible. Each rejection is reported through a distinct skip trace category covering unsuitable, shared read-only, and inaccessible cases.

Per-range balancing state holds a start sequence, a next eligible scan time, a periodic identifier-reset deadline, a previous sequence marker, and a two-slot active identifier history. The start sequence is captured from the address space at allocation, the next scan is delayed by a configurable scan delay, the reset deadline extends further by a fixed reset period, and the previous marker starts one behind current to avoid premature skipping.

Range scanning moves through delayed start, periodic reset, once-per-sequence guard, access gating, and forced retry. New ranges wait until their deadline, old ranges rotate identifier history on expiry, ranges already visited in the current sequence advance the global offset and are skipped, ranges without recorded access are deferred unless no other candidate exists, when a second pass forces one range to preserve forward progress.

Scanning advances in huge-page-aligned windows bounded by separate budgets for modified pages and virtual pages, relinquishing the processor between windows. Completion marks the range visited for the sequence and, when forcing, stops after one range. The address-space offset is left at the stopping point when ranges remain, otherwise the scan position is reset. Time spent scanning throttles future scans by scaling observed runtime by thirty-two into the task stamp, bounding overhead near three percent.

The range walk occurs under the address-space read lock and releases it once the stopping position is recorded. Allocation races for per-range state are resolved with an atomic compare exchange where the loser frees its allocation. Processor relinquish points are permitted inside the window loop while the read lock is held.

Periodic NUMA evaluation is driven from the tick for tasks with an address space that are neither exiting nor kernel threads and whose deferred work item is idle. It compares execution runtime against a stamp plus a millisecond-based period, initializes the period on first use, advances the stamp, and queues resumable deferred work only when the address-space next-scan time has arrived.

Migration across nodes restarts the scan period unless balancing is disabled, the task lacks an address space or fault history, is exiting, or stays on the same node. After at least one scan, moves toward the preferred node or moves where the source was not already the preferred node leave the period unchanged; other cross-node moves restart it.

Alternate builds provide empty definitions for periodic NUMA evaluation, NUMA enqueue accounting, scan-period update, offline group cleanup, and load-average lag migration, preserving call sites while disabling the corresponding behavior.

Enqueue accounting verifies the queue matches the entity, adds the entity weight to the queue load, and increments the queued count. For task entities it additionally performs NUMA and last-level-cache enqueue bookkeeping and links the entity into the run-queue task list.

Signed accumulation uses single-access loads and stores and clamps negative underflow to zero instead of wrapping, so concurrent observers see either the old or new value but concurrent writers can lose updates.

Weight changes preserve lag by scaling virtual lag, relative deadline offset, and optionally virtual protection in proportion of old to new weight using wide division. The design keeps the weighted average virtual time across the queue stable, adjusting the entity virtual time implicitly through scaled lag rather than moving the average.

Online reweighting converts absolute deadline and protection markers to queue-average-relative form, captures current lag, temporarily removes the entity from ordering and queued accounting when not current, applies proportional rescaling and load update, then restores absolute markers and reinserts. Offline entities only rescale and update load. Equal weights are a no-op.

Hierarchical proportional weight multiplies the incoming weight by the entity load share and normalizes by the parent queue load except at the root where it normalizes by the baseline nice-zero load, with a lower bound at the minimum share.

Task fair-weight updates refresh the current clock when queued, reweight the leaf entity, refresh cached inverse weight, and when queued propagate proportional weights upward through ancestors to recompute the root fair share for deadline-based ordering.

Symmetric-multiprocessing shares derive queue load as the larger of scaled instantaneous weight and averaged load, reconstruct group weight by replacing the local contribution with current load, compute proportional shares from group shares, and clamp between minimum and caller-supplied maximum to support small-share partitioning.

Group sizing counts online processors, narrowed to the group cpuset when cpusets are enabled, and estimates runnable tasks from shifted runnable average, each floored at one so empty cpusets or idle groups cannot yield zero divisors or defeat minimum-share clamping.

Five share helpers select different scaling numerators and ceilings from the same core estimator: task-count scaling, processor-count scaling capped by highest-priority weight, concurrent minimum of the two scalings, direct group-share scaling, and unwrapped group shares without estimation.

Contribution withdrawal skips the root group, then atomically subtracts both load and runnable contributions from group totals, clears local contributions, and stamps the update time with the owning run-queue clock, leaving the caller responsible for run-queue stability.

Offline cleanup requires the run queue to be held, brackets the walk with a loop clock-update region to avoid redundant clock steps, holds read-side critical section protection while iterating all groups, and clears each processor-local fair queue contribution.

Load-average lag migration only acts when the entity average has not decayed and the source processor is idle, estimating current time from idle-captured physical and proportional clocks minus throttled time with ordered loads that prefer underestimation, falling back to the queue last-update time when newer, then adding elapsed physical time since idle before refreshing the blocked entity average; fully throttled queues are left untouched.
Sixty-four-bit values split for thirty-two-bit access are read through a wrapper that fetches the value together with its copy slot to obtain a consistent snapshot.
Estimated-utilization margin is one percent of the scheduler capacity scale.
Five operation flags occupy successive low bits with values 0x01 for group update, 0x02 for skip aging, 0x04 for attach, 0x08 for detach, and 0x10 for utilization-estimate update.

Estimated utilization accounting is gated by a scheduler feature flag. Enqueue adds the task estimate to the queue estimate and dequeue subtracts it clamped to avoid underflow, both with single-access stores followed by a tracepoint.

Fair parameter installation derives static priority from the requested nice value and selects a scheduling slice: a caller-provided runtime enables custom-slice mode with clamping between one tenth of a millisecond and one hundred milliseconds, otherwise custom mode is cleared and the global base slice is used.

Entity placement refreshes non-custom slices from the global base, derives a weight-normalized slice, and discounts the already-queued case from the queue count. When lag placement is enabled with a non-empty queue and nonzero stored lag, it prepares to inflate the stored lag to compensate for averaging dilution caused by insertion.
